strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: instead of modeling the static Boltzmann distribution or reconstructing time-lagged frames via autoencoders, the paper conditions a Boltzmann-generator-style flow-matching model on a learned low-dimensional embedding of the current configuration to predict the time-lagged distribution, using the conditioning bottleneck itself as the CV. This is a reasonably creative synthesis of ideas from Boltzmann generators/flow matching and time-lagged CV learning (TAE/VDE/DeepTICA).

The evaluation spans two distinct and practically relevant downstream enhanced-sampling tasks (SMD and OPES), which test different desiderata for CVs (transition-path quality vs. equilibrium state discrimination), giving a more holistic picture than single-task evaluations common in prior MLCV papers.

Reasonably thorough set of baselines (DeepLDA, DeepTDA, DeepTICA, TAE, VDE) covering both supervised and self-supervised/time-lagged families, with consistent training data and comparable model capacity (hidden dim, similar layer counts).

Useful ablations isolating the contribution of the autocorrelation loss and the RMSD-aligned Cartesian coordinate representation versus heavy-atom-distance features, along with sensitivity analyses tying learned CVs back to interpretable atomic features.
Good methodological detail and appendix documentation (simulation engines, force fields, time steps, hyperparameter search ranges), aiding reproducibility for the specific system studied.

The SMD results show a substantial and qualitatively convincing improvement in transition-state energy (much lower than baselines), suggesting TLC does capture more physically realistic transition pathways in this case.
weaknesses: The entire empirical validation is restricted to a single, very small toy system (Alanine Dipeptide, 22 atoms, 1-D CV). Given the paper's stated motivation (drug discovery, protein folding, materials science), the lack of any experiment on a larger or more realistic system substantially limits the evidence for significance/generalizability of the method.

OPES results are mixed and not clearly favorable to TLC: in Table 2, TLC's free-energy difference (9.83 ± 1.15) is not closer to the reference (10.06 ± 0.22) than several baselines (e.g., DeepTDA 10.01 ± 0.49, DeepTICA 9.99 ± 0.21, VDE 10.11 ± 0.28), and TLC has notably higher variance. This undercuts the abstract's claim of "equal or superior performance" for the OPES task specifically.

In the SMD comparison (Table 1), the force constant k differs substantially across methods (300 for TLC vs. up to 1200 for TAE, 700 for VDE), chosen via a search under an energy threshold. Because the threshold and search criterion directly affect the RMSD/THP/energy tradeoff, it is unclear whether the comparison isolates CV quality versus simply reflects different operating points on each method's own hyperparameter curve; a Pareto-front style comparison across k would be more convincing.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core idea largely amounts to swapping the decoder/reconstruction objective of TAE/VDE with a conditional flow-matching generative objective borrowed from existing Boltzmann generator work (TBG), plus an autocorrelation loss adapted from VDE. The conceptual delta over prior time-lagged CV methods is real but modest.

No exploration of CVs with dimensionality greater than 1, despite many real systems requiring multi-dimensional CVs; it is unclear whether the conditioning/flow-matching approach scales to higher-dimensional or more complex CV spaces.

Key hyperparameters (e.g., λ for the autocorrelation loss, EGNN architecture details, training schedule/compute cost of the generative backbone) are not clearly specified, and the added computational cost of training a full generative model (versus a simple encoder/autoencoder as in prior MLCV baselines) is not discussed or compared, which matters for practical adoption.

Results are averaged over a relatively small number of seeds/trajectories in some analyses (e.g., 4 OPES seeds), and no statistical significance tests are reported to substantiate claims of TLC's superiority given overlapping error bars in several tables/figures.

The paper does not compare against other recent generative or diffusion-based CV/transition-path methods beyond the classical MLCV baselines (e.g., no comparison to diffusion path samplers or other generative transition-path approaches cited in related work), which would better contextualize the contribution relative to the current state of the art.

strengths: The core idea of learning CVs by conditioning a time-lagged generative (flow-matching) model, rather than only discriminating or reconstructing configurations, is a reasonably novel angle that connects Boltzmann generator technology with the CV discovery literature.
The paper is well organized, with clear background on enhanced sampling, CVs, and prior ML-CV methods, making the motivation for time-lagged modeling understandable.

A fairly comprehensive set of baselines is compared (DeepLDA, DeepTDA, DeepTICA, TAE, VDE) across two different enhanced-sampling protocols (SMD and OPES), together with several complementary metrics (RMSD, THP, transition-state energy, free-energy surface, free-energy convergence, sensitivity analysis).
Ablation studies are provided for the two key design choices (autocorrelation loss and RMSD-aligned Cartesian input vs. heavy-atom distances), giving some insight into what drives performance.
Visualizations (Ramachandran plots, FES curves, phi-time traces) are informative and allow qualitative comparison across methods.
weaknesses: Validation is restricted to a single, extremely small toy system (alanine dipeptide, 22 atoms) with known ground-truth CVs (phi/psi). This is far from representative of the larger, more complex systems (protein folding, ligand binding) motivating the paper in the introduction, and it is unclear whether the proposed generative-conditioning approach scales computationally or statistically to such systems.

Results are mixed rather than consistently favorable: DeepTICA achieves the best RMSD in SMD, VDE is closest to the reference free-energy difference in OPES (Table 2), and TAE also identifies three metastable basins in the FES like TLC. The paper's framing of "equal or superior performance" is generous given these inconsistencies.

The SMD comparison tunes the force constant k separately and differently for each method, with the paper reporting "the highest success rate under a maximum energy threshold" — this ad hoc selection procedure raises fairness/reproducibility concerns and could bias results in TLC's favor.

The ablation study undermines the paper's own claimed design contributions: removing the autocorrelation loss actually improves THP substantially (97.27 vs. 60.93 for full TLC), suggesting the proposed loss's benefit is not robustly established and results are sensitive to hyperparameter/loss choices in ways not fully explored.

Error bars/variance are large in several key results (e.g., E_TS = 33.58 ± 15.19, ∆F = 9.83 ± 1.15 with only 4 seeds), and several qualitative results (Figure 6 phi-distribution) are based on a single simulation per method, limiting statistical confidence in the comparisons.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely combines an existing generative backbone (TBG/flow matching), the time-lagged encoder idea from TAE, and the autocorrelation loss from VDE, without a strong new theoretical justification for why time-lagged generative conditioning should outperform time-lagged reconstruction (TAE) or covariance-based (DeepTICA) approaches beyond empirical trial.

No analysis of computational cost/training overhead is provided; training a full equivariant generative flow model to learn a scalar CV is likely far more expensive than simple MLP-based baselines (DeepLDA, DeepTDA, TAE, VDE), and this tradeoff is not discussed or justified.

The invariant-representation strategy (aligning every configuration to a single reference C5 state via Kabsch) may not generalize to systems with multiple conformational basins or larger molecules where a single rigid-body reference alignment is ill-defined, but this limitation is not discussed.

Missing comparison or discussion relative to more recent CV-free/generative transition-path methods (e.g., Holdijk et al. 2023, cited but not empirically compared), which would better contextualize the contribution relative to the broader landscape of ML-based rare-event sampling.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually interesting extension of time-lagged CV learning (à la TAE) by replacing the reconstruction decoder with a conditional flow-matching generative model built on transferable Boltzmann generators, allowing the encoder to be trained end-to-end via a proper conditional distribution objective rather than simple reconstruction.

Evaluation spans two distinct and practically relevant downstream tasks (steered MD and OPES), rather than only visualizing the CV landscape, which gives a more application-grounded assessment of CV quality.
Includes a reasonably comprehensive set of baselines (DeepLDA, DeepTDA, DeepTICA, TAE, VDE) covering both supervised and time-lagged self-supervised paradigms.

Provides useful ablations isolating the contribution of the autocorrelation loss and the RMSD-aligned coordinate representation, along with sensitivity analysis of the learned CV against input features.

TLC achieves a notably lower transition-state energy in SMD experiments, suggesting the learned CV better respects the true energy barrier location (crossing near φ=0) rather than ignoring it, which is a meaningful qualitative result.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on a single, extremely small toy system (22-atom alanine dipeptide in vacuum-like tip3p solvent with just two known ground-truth CVs). No results on a larger peptide, protein, or condensed-phase system are given, leaving scalability and generality of the approach essentially unaddressed.

Results are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: DeepTICA has better RMSD in SMD, TAE has comparable THP, and in the OPES free-energy-difference metric (Table 2) TLC is not the closest to the reference (VDE and DeepTDA are closer), undermining the claim of consistent superiority.

The free-energy surface for TLC shows three metastable basins along the learned CV (Figure 5f) even though the true system only has two metastable states; this is framed positively (matching TAE) but could equally indicate a spurious/artificial basin, and this ambiguity is not analyzed further.

The comparison across baselines is potentially confounded by inconsistent input representations: distance-based baselines (DeepLDA/DeepTDA/DeepTICA) use heavy-atom distances, while TAE/VDE/TLC use RMSD-aligned Cartesian coordinates. Since the paper's own ablation shows input representation strongly affects performance, it is unclear how much of TLC's advantage stems from the generative modeling contribution versus the representation choice, since baselines were not re-run with the same representation.

No exploration or sensitivity analysis of the time-lag hyperparameter τ, which is a critical and often sensitive choice for time-lagged CV methods; only a single fixed value (1000 fs) is used throughout.

Statistical robustness is limited: SMD results (Table 1) appear to come from a single trained model per method (no seeds/error bars for RMSD/THP), and the OPES results are averaged over only 4 seeds, which is a small sample for a method with reportedly high variance (e.g., TLC's ΔF std of 1.15 vs DeepTDA's 0.49).

The method's novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely substitutes a flow-matching Boltzmann generator decoder in place of an autoencoder/VAE decoder within the existing time-lagged CV learning paradigm (TAE/VDE), without a strong theoretical or conceptual leap beyond this substitution.

Computational cost of training a full generative (EGNN-based flow-matching) model compared to lightweight MLP baselines is not discussed or benchmarked, which is relevant for practical adoption of the method.

strengths: Novel repurposing of a molecular foundation model (BioEmu) as a time-lagged conditional generator to learn slow collective variables (CVs), extending ideas from conditioning-adapter literature (e.g., ControlNet-style adapters) to a new and relevant scientific domain.

Unusually thorough and systematic empirical evaluation compared to prior MLCV work: three fast-folding proteins (larger than the commonly used alanine dipeptide), two distinct downstream enhanced-sampling tasks (OPES free-energy estimation and steered-MD transition path sampling), and three established self-supervised baselines (DeepTICA, TAE, VDE) retrained under matched conditions using the mlcolvar library.

Rich interpretability analysis beyond raw task metrics: sensitivity analysis on Cα-distances, secondary-structure correlation, committor-function correlation, meta-stable state discrimination, and VAMP scores, giving a fairly complete picture of what the learned CVs capture.

Extensive and informative ablation studies (time-lagged conditioning vs. non-time-lagged, frozen vs. unfrozen backbone, encoder size/placement, effect of mixing with Cα-RMSD in SMD, higher-dimensional CVs, an additional alanine dipeptide multi-pathway test with a different backbone) that support several of the paper's design choices.

Detailed reproducibility statement, transparent reporting of simulation configurations (OPES/SMD hyperparameters, force fields, data splits), and honest discussion of failure cases/limitations (e.g., non-convergence in longer OPES runs, VAMP score caveats).
weaknesses: Quantitative results are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: BioEmu-CV is not always best on PMF MAE (e.g., Chignolin) or committor correlation (VDE scores higher), and VAMP scores do not clearly favor the proposed method, which the authors themselves partially discount as an unreliable metric.

Evidence of incomplete convergence undermines the central free-energy evaluation: the 1 μs OPES runs show large standard deviations, and the appendix experiment with a ~10x longer (9.8 μs) simulation shows even the best baseline still fails to converge, raising doubts about whether the 1 μs-based comparisons in the main results are statistically reliable.

Test systems remain small (10–28 residues); despite the claim of being 'larger than Alanine Dipeptide,' these are still tiny, well-studied fast-folding peptides, so scalability/generalization to realistically sized proteins or more complex biomolecular systems (where CV learning is most needed) is not demonstrated.

Methodological novelty is relatively incremental: the core idea largely combines an existing adapter-conditioning technique (from text-to-image diffusion literature) with an existing time-lagged self-supervised objective (conceptually close to VDE), applied to a new backbone; the main contribution is engineering integration and benchmarking rather than a fundamentally new learning principle.

The approach is tightly coupled to the quality and coverage of the pretrained BioEmu model, and it is unclear how CV quality would degrade for protein families or state spaces not well represented in BioEmu's training distribution.

The method requires very large computational budgets for evaluation (~8,000 GPU-hours per protein for a single OPES evaluation), which may limit accessibility and thorough reproducibility/validation by others despite the detailed configuration tables provided.

CV dimensionality is fixed to one for the main experiments, with higher-dimensional CVs relegated to a small qualitative appendix study on a single protein (BBA) without quantitative downstream-task comparison, leaving open whether the method scales to more expressive multi-dimensional CVs.

strengths: The core idea of repurposing BioEmu's conditioning pathway and time-lagged generative objective to learn collective variables (CVs) is a reasonable and relatively novel way to leverage a pretrained molecular foundation model for enhanced sampling, extending the spirit of VDE-style time-lagged encoders to a diffusion-based generative backbone.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this subfield: it covers OPES free-energy estimation, steered MD transition-path sampling, sensitivity analysis, secondary-structure correlation, meta-stable state discrimination, committor-function correlation, VAMP scores, alanine dipeptide multi-pathway capture, and several ablations (time-lag vs. no time-lag, frozen vs. unfrozen BioEmu weights, encoder size, conditioning placement, CV dimensionality).

The paper explicitly attempts to create a standardized, side-by-side comparison of several ML-CV baselines (DeepTICA, TAE, VDE) on fast-folding proteins larger than alanine dipeptide, which is a useful community contribution if the benchmark is reliable and reproducible.

Reasonably detailed reproducibility/appendix material (simulation configurations, hyperparameters, dataset description) is provided, and an ablation study isolates the contribution of time-lagged conditioning and weight freezing.
Qualitative analyses (sensitivity maps, secondary-structure correlation, committor correlation) attempt to go beyond aggregate numbers and probe physical interpretability of the learned CVs.
weaknesses: Quantitative results are mixed rather than consistently favorable: in Table 1, BioEmu-CV is not uniformly best (e.g., DeepTICA has lower PMF MAE for Chignolin), and the reported standard deviations for ΔF are often larger than the differences between methods (e.g., ±3.97 to ±5.43 kJ/mol spread versus sub-kJ/mol differences in mean |ΔF_ref − ΔF|), which raises doubts about the statistical significance of the claimed improvements.

In the VAMP-score and committor-correlation comparisons (Table 10, Table 4), BioEmu-CV is not clearly superior to VDE or DeepTICA, undermining the claim that it best captures the slow dynamical modes.

The steered-MD evaluation mixes the learned CV with an explicit Cα-RMSD term in a 5:5 ratio (Appendix B.4/D.3), which confounds the contribution of the learned CV itself; the D.3 ablation shows that without this RMSD term, BioEmu-CV (like most baselines) largely fails to reach the target state, suggesting much of the reported SMD success may be driven by the hand-crafted RMSD component rather than the learned CV.

The benchmark is limited to three very small fast-folding proteins (10–28 residues) plus alanine dipeptide; despite the claim of being a benchmark for proteins "larger than alanine dipeptide," this is still a narrow regime and does not demonstrate scalability to realistically sized proteins, limiting the significance of the contribution.

The method is computationally very expensive (reported ~8,000 GPU-hours per OPES evaluation), which may limit practical adoption and reproducibility outside well-resourced groups, and is not clearly justified as scaling better than simpler/cheaper baselines (e.g., TICA performs competitively in some ablations, Appendix C.5).

Longer OPES simulations (Appendix C.8) do not improve convergence and reveal persistent sampling gaps, raising concerns about whether the 1 μs results used for the main comparison are adequately converged for drawing firm conclusions.

The methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely combines existing ingredients (adapter-style conditioning from T2I-Adapter, time-lagged reconstruction from VDE, and a frozen pretrained generative backbone) without a strong theoretical justification for why diffusion-based time-lagged generation should yield better CVs than prior simpler objectives, and the empirical gains do not strongly support this claim.

strengths: Proposes a novel and conceptually clean way to extract collective variables (CVs) by re-purposing a pretrained molecular foundation model (BioEmu) with a lightweight, time-lagged conditioning encoder, avoiding training a dedicated CV model from scratch.

Provides the first systematic, head-to-head benchmark of several self-supervised MLCV methods (DeepTICA, TAE, VDE) against the proposed BioEmu-CV on three fast-folding proteins larger than alanine dipeptide, using two distinct downstream enhanced-sampling tasks (OPES free-energy estimation and steered-MD transition path sampling).

Extensive and carefully documented appendix: data/trajectory details, OPES and SMD configurations, sensitivity analysis, secondary-structure analysis, committor-function correlation, VAMP scores, simple PCA/TICA baselines, alanine dipeptide multi-pathway test, high-dimensional CV extension, and multiple ablations (time-lag necessity, frozen vs. unfrozen BioEmu, encoder size/placement, effect of RMSD mixing) — this greatly strengthens reproducibility and the depth of evidence.
Interpretability analyses (sensitivity maps, secondary structure correspondence, committor correlation) give some physical grounding to the learned CVs beyond pure downstream task metrics.

Transition-path sampling results (Table 2) show a clear and fairly convincing advantage for BioEmu-CV in hit percentage and transition-state energy across all three proteins, which is a meaningful practical outcome.
weaknesses: The free-energy estimation results (Table 1, Figure 2, Figure 10) are mixed: BioEmu-CV is not uniformly best (e.g., PMF MAE is worse than DeepTICA for Chignolin, and large error bars across methods for Trp-cage/BBA suggest none of the methods, including BioEmu-CV, convincingly converge), weakening the central claim of superior slow-mode capture.

A potentially important confound is not addressed: BioEmu is pretrained on a large, diverse corpus of protein structures/dynamics, whereas the baselines (DeepTICA, TAE, VDE) are trained from scratch solely on the limited trajectory of each individual protein. The comparison may therefore partly reflect the benefit of large-scale pretraining/data leakage rather than the proposed time-lagged conditioning mechanism itself; it is unclear whether BioEmu's training set overlaps with or strongly informs these benchmark proteins.

The ablation in Table 13 shows that removing the time-lagged conditioning (using instantaneous reconstruction instead) yields comparable or even slightly better ∆F and THP in some metrics, raising questions about how much of the method's performance is actually attributable to the key proposed idea (time-lagged generation) versus simply using BioEmu's frozen representations.

Evaluation is restricted to three small fast-folding proteins (10–28 residues); while larger than alanine dipeptide, this is still far from realistic drug-discovery-scale systems, so claims of scalability remain only partially substantiated.

Interpretability metrics are sometimes ambiguous or contradict the main narrative, e.g., VDE achieves the highest committor correlation (0.778) in Table 4, slightly above BioEmu-CV (0.748), and VAMP scores in Table 10 do not show BioEmu-CV as clearly superior, undercutting the claim that BioEmu-CV best captures the slow dynamical modes.

The method's CV dimensionality is fixed to one throughout the main experiments, with only a brief qualitative extension to 4D in the appendix; it is unclear how well the approach generalizes to higher-dimensional CVs needed for more complex systems.

Writing and presentation have some rough edges (e.g., occasional unclear phrasing, dense figures with many sub-panels that are hard to parse), and the overall novelty is somewhat incremental — the core idea largely adapts existing adapter-based conditioning techniques (e.g., T2I-Adapter) to a new domain rather than introducing fundamentally new modeling techniques.
